blocks.text: Carbohydrates: classification

Biomolecules are the organic compounds that make up living cells and carry out the processes of life: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, enzymes, hormones and nucleic acids. This unit studies the chemistry of each, at the level of NCERT Class 12.

**Carbohydrates** were once thought to be hydrates of carbon, $\mathrm{C_x(H_2O)_y}$, which explains the name, but the modern definition is structural. They supply energy, act as stored food (starch, glycogen) and form structural material (cellulose).

An optically active **polyhydroxy aldehyde or polyhydroxy ketone**, or a compound that gives such a unit on hydrolysis. Glucose, $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}$, is a polyhydroxy aldehyde (an aldose); fructose is a polyhydroxy ketone (a ketose).

**Classification by hydrolysis.**

- **Monosaccharides** cannot be hydrolysed to simpler carbohydrates. They are named by the number of carbons (triose, tetrose, pentose, hexose) and by the carbonyl group: an **aldose** has an aldehyde group, a **ketose** a ketone group. Glucose is an aldohexose; fructose is a ketohexose; ribose is an aldopentose.
- **Oligosaccharides** give 2 to 10 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis. **Disaccharides** (sucrose, maltose, lactose) give two.
- **Polysaccharides** give a large number of monosaccharide units (starch, cellulose, glycogen).

**Classification by taste and solubility.** Monosaccharides and oligosaccharides are sweet, crystalline and soluble in water; they are called **sugars**. Polysaccharides are not sweet and are called **non-sugars**.

**Classification by reducing action.** Carbohydrates that reduce Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent are **reducing sugars** (all monosaccharides, maltose, lactose). Those that do not are **non-reducing sugars** (sucrose).

blocks.text: What to learn from this figure: The first split is by what hydrolysis gives, not by taste: none, two to ten units, or many units. Then the aldehyde or ketone group splits monosaccharides into aldoses and ketoses.
Methods of preparation of glucose

Glucose, also called dextrose or grape sugar, is the most important monosaccharide. It is prepared in two ways.

**1. From sucrose.** On boiling sucrose with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid in an alcoholic solution, glucose and fructose are formed in equal amounts.
Acid hydrolysis of sucrose gives an equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose.
**2. From starch (commercial method).** Starch is hydrolysed by boiling with dilute sulfuric acid at 393 K under a pressure of 2 to 3 atmospheres.
Starch is a polymer of glucose, so complete hydrolysis gives only glucose.
Structure of glucose

The structure of glucose was worked out from its reactions. Each experiment points to one structural feature:

- Prolonged heating with hydroiodic acid gives **n-hexane**, so the six carbons are in a **straight, unbranched chain**.
- It forms a cyanohydrin with HCN and an oxime with hydroxylamine, so it contains a **carbonyl group**.
- Mild oxidation with bromine water gives **gluconic acid** ($\mathrm{C_6}$ monocarboxylic acid), showing the carbonyl group is an **aldehyde** (it is at carbon 1).
- Oxidation with nitric acid gives **saccharic acid**, a dicarboxylic acid, so there is also a **primary alcohol group** at the other end.
- Acetylation with acetic anhydride gives a **pentaacetate**, so there are **five hydroxyl groups**, one on each of the other carbons.

Together these give the open-chain structure of glucose: 2,3,4,5,6-pentahydroxyhexanal, $\mathrm{HOCH_2-(CHOH)_4-CHO}$.

**Why the open-chain form is not enough.** Glucose does not give Schiff's test or the sodium hydrogensulfite addition product, and its pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine, which means the free aldehyde group is largely absent. It also exists in two forms, with different specific rotations, which interconvert in solution. The explanation is that the $\mathrm{-CHO}$ at C-1 reacts with the $\mathrm{-OH}$ at C-5 to form a six-membered ring containing one oxygen atom, a cyclic **hemiacetal**. The ring resembles pyran, so this form is called the **pyranose** form.

The new hydroxyl group at C-1 can lie on either side of the ring. The two ring forms, which differ only in the configuration at **C-1 (the anomeric carbon)**, are called **anomers**: $\alpha$-D-glucopyranose (specific rotation $+111^\circ$) and $\beta$-D-glucopyranose ($+19.2^\circ$). When either dissolves in water, the optical rotation slowly changes until it reaches an equilibrium value of $+52.5^\circ$. This change is called **mutarotation**. The equilibrium mixture contains mainly the two cyclic forms with very little of the open chain.

What to learn from this figure: Glucose in water is mostly a ring, not an open chain: the C-5 hydroxyl closes onto the C-1 aldehyde carbon. The new OH at C-1 can point down (alpha) or up (beta), and that is the only difference between the two anomers.

blocks.text: The $\alpha$ and $\beta$ forms of glucose are **anomers**, not enantiomers: they differ only at C-1. Do not mix up the $\alpha/\beta$ labels with the D/L labels, which describe a different carbon (C-5).
D and L configuration of monosaccharides

The prefixes **D** and **L** show the configuration of the stereocentre farthest from the carbonyl group, relative to glyceraldehyde, which was chosen as the reference. In the Fischer projection, with the aldehyde at the top, the molecule is **D** if the $\mathrm{-OH}$ on that carbon is on the **right** and **L** if it is on the **left**. For glucose this carbon is C-5. Naturally occurring monosaccharides almost all belong to the D-series.

The D/L label is **not** the direction of optical rotation. The sign (+) means dextrorotatory and (-) laevorotatory, and is found only by experiment. Thus natural glucose is D-(+)-glucose and natural fructose is D-(-)-fructose: both are D, but one rotates light to the right and the other to the left. In the open chain Fischer projection of D-glucose the $\mathrm{-OH}$ groups on C-2, C-4 and C-5 are on the right and that on C-3 on the left.

An aldohexose has four stereocentres (C-2 to C-5), so there are $2^4 = 16$ stereoisomers, of which 8 are D and 8 are L. A ketohexose has three stereocentres (C-3 to C-5), so there are $2^3 = 8$ stereoisomers.

blocks.problem: An aldohexose is written in open-chain form. (a) How many optical isomers does it have? (b) How many of these belong to the D-series? (c) How many does the open-chain ketohexose fructose have?
blocks.solution:
(a) Count the stereogenic centres. In $\mathrm{HOCH_2-CHOH-CHOH-CHOH-CHOH-CHO}$, C-2, C-3, C-4 and C-5 each carry four different groups. C-1 (aldehyde) and C-6 (primary alcohol) are not stereogenic. With $n = 4$ stereocentres the number of optical isomers is $2^n = 2^4 = 16$.

(b) Half have the C-5 hydroxyl on the right (D) and half on the left (L), so 8 are D-isomers.

(c) In fructose the carbonyl is at C-2, so C-1 and C-2 and C-6 are not stereogenic; only C-3, C-4 and C-5 are. Therefore $2^3 = 8$ optical isomers.

blocks.text: Fructose: preparation and structure

**Method of preparation of fructose.** Fructose is obtained along with glucose when sucrose is hydrolysed by acid or the enzyme invertase (see the equation above). The two sugars can be separated, for example as their calcium salts or by crystallisation.

**Structure of fructose.** Fructose has the same molecular formula as glucose, $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}$, but is a **ketohexose**, 1,3,4,5,6-pentahydroxyhexan-2-one, $\mathrm{HOCH_2-CO-(CHOH)_3-CH_2OH}$, in which the carbonyl group is at C-2. It is laevorotatory, with a specific rotation of $-92.4^\circ$, and is called D-(-)-fructose (also laevulose). It is the **sweetest** of all natural sugars and is found in honey and fruits.

Like glucose, fructose forms a cyclic hemiacetal (a hemiketal), but here the ketone carbon C-2 reacts with the hydroxyl on **C-5**, giving a **five-membered ring** that resembles furan, called the **furanose** form. The anomers are $\alpha$-D-fructofuranose and $\beta$-D-fructofuranose. In alkaline solution fructose isomerises into glucose and mannose (enolisation), so it also reduces Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution even though it is a ketose.

blocks.problem: The specific rotation of sucrose is $+66.5^\circ$, that of D-glucose is $+52.5^\circ$ and that of D-fructose is $-92.4^\circ$. Sucrose is hydrolysed completely. Calculate the specific rotation of the resulting equimolar mixture (taking the average) and explain why it is called invert sugar.
blocks.solution:
Hydrolysis of one mole of sucrose gives one mole of glucose and one mole of fructose, so the two sugars are present in equimolar amounts. Taking the mean of the rotations,

$$[\alpha] = \frac{(+52.5) + (-92.4)}{2} = \frac{-39.9}{2} = -19.95^\circ$$

The mixture is therefore laevorotatory. Because the sign of rotation changes from dextro (+66.5 degrees) in sucrose to laevo (about -20 degrees) in the product, the optical rotation has been **inverted**, so the mixture is called invert sugar and the hydrolysing enzyme is invertase.

blocks.text: Disaccharides: sucrose, maltose and lactose

Two monosaccharides are joined by an oxygen bridge between their carbon atoms, called a **glycosidic linkage**, with loss of a molecule of water. The sugars react through their hemiacetal (anomeric) hydroxyl groups.
The $\mathrm{C-O-C}$ link formed when the anomeric hydroxyl of one monosaccharide condenses with a hydroxyl group of another, joining them into a disaccharide or polysaccharide with loss of water.

**Sucrose** (table sugar, from sugarcane and sugar beet) is made of **$\alpha$-D-glucose and $\beta$-D-fructose** joined by an **$\alpha$-1,$\beta$-2 glycosidic linkage**, which uses both anomeric carbons (C-1 of glucose and C-2 of fructose). Since neither unit has a free hemiacetal group, sucrose is a **non-reducing sugar**. It is dextrorotatory, and on hydrolysis gives glucose and fructose (invert sugar).

**Maltose** (malt sugar) is made of **two $\alpha$-D-glucose units** joined by an **$\alpha$-1,4 glycosidic linkage** (C-1 of one unit to C-4 of the other). One unit still has a free anomeric carbon, so maltose is a **reducing sugar**. It is produced by the action of diastase (amylase) on starch and is hydrolysed to two glucose units by maltase.

**Lactose** (milk sugar, about 5 per cent of cow's milk) is made of **$\beta$-D-galactose and $\beta$-D-glucose** joined by a **$\beta$-1,4 glycosidic linkage** between C-1 of galactose and C-4 of glucose. It has a free anomeric carbon on the glucose unit and is a **reducing sugar**. It is hydrolysed by lactase.

blocks.problem: A disaccharide X gives only D-glucose on hydrolysis, reduces Tollens' reagent and is obtained when starch is acted on by diastase. Another disaccharide Y gives glucose and fructose and does not reduce Tollens' reagent. Identify X and Y, give their linkages and explain the difference in reducing behaviour.
blocks.solution:
X gives only glucose, so both units are glucose; it is formed from starch by diastase (amylase) and is reducing, so it is **maltose**, $\alpha$-D-glucose with $\alpha$-D-glucose through an $\alpha$-1,4 glycosidic linkage. The second glucose unit retains a free hemiacetal (anomeric) carbon, which can open to give an aldehyde group, so maltose reduces Tollens' reagent.

Y gives glucose and fructose and does not reduce, so it is **sucrose**, with an $\alpha$-1,$\beta$-2 linkage. The linkage joins C-1 of glucose to C-2 of fructose, which means both anomeric carbons are tied up in the bond and no free aldehyde or ketone can form, so sucrose is non-reducing.
blocks.answer: X = maltose ($\alpha$-1,4); Y = sucrose ($\alpha$-1,$\beta$-2). Sucrose is non-reducing because both anomeric carbons form the glycosidic bond.

blocks.text: Polysaccharides: starch, cellulose and glycogen

Polysaccharides are long polymers of monosaccharide units held by glycosidic linkages. They are tasteless, do not reduce Tollens' reagent and are not sweet.

**Starch** is the chief food storage polysaccharide of plants (rice, wheat, potatoes, maize). It is a mixture of two components, both polymers of **$\alpha$-D-glucose**.

- **Amylose** (about 15-20 per cent): a long, **unbranched** chain with **$\alpha$-1,4** glycosidic linkages. It is **soluble in water** and gives the blue colour with iodine.
- **Amylopectin** (about 80-85 per cent): a **branched** chain with $\alpha$-1,4 linkages in the chains and **$\alpha$-1,6** linkages at the branch points. It is **insoluble in water**.

**Cellulose** is the chief structural material of plant cell walls (cotton is almost pure cellulose). It is a straight-chain polymer of **$\beta$-D-glucose** joined by **$\beta$-1,4** glycosidic linkages. Humans cannot digest cellulose because we lack the enzyme (cellulase) needed to break the $\beta$-linkage, while many herbivores can because bacteria in their gut supply it.

**Glycogen** is the carbohydrate stored in **animal** bodies, called animal starch. It is found in the liver, muscles and brain. Like amylopectin it is a polymer of $\alpha$-D-glucose with $\alpha$-1,4 and $\alpha$-1,6 linkages, but it is **more highly branched**. When the body needs glucose, glycogen is broken down into it.

The difference between starch and cellulose is only the **configuration of the glycosidic link**: $\alpha$ in starch and $\beta$ in cellulose. This is a favourite examination question; the other common one is "which polysaccharide has branches?" (amylopectin and glycogen).
Importance of carbohydrates

Carbohydrates are the main source of **energy** for living organisms: glucose in the blood is oxidised to release energy. Starch and glycogen act as **stored food** in plants and animals. Cellulose gives **structural strength** to plants and is used for paper, cotton and wood, and is also dietary fibre. Sugars such as honey, sucrose and fruit sugars are important foods and sweeteners; lactose is the sugar of milk; ribose and deoxyribose form part of **nucleic acids** (RNA and DNA). Fermentation of sugars gives ethanol, and carbohydrate derivatives such as cellulose esters are used in making fibres and films.
Carbohydrates: polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. Reducing sugars: glucose, fructose, maltose, lactose. Non-reducing: sucrose. Starch (alpha), glycogen (alpha, more branched), cellulose (beta-1,4).
Amino acids and their classifications
A compound containing both an amino group and a carboxyl group, with the amino group on the carbon next to the $\mathrm{-COOH}$ (the $\alpha$-carbon). General formula $\mathrm{R-CH(NH_2)-COOH}$.

Proteins are polymers of about **twenty** standard $\alpha$-amino acids. All the natural ones in proteins belong to the **L-series**. Except glycine ($\mathrm{R=H}$), the $\alpha$-carbon is a stereocentre, so they are optically active; glycine is **optically inactive**.

**Classification by the nature of the side chain R.**

- **Neutral** amino acids have one amino and one carboxyl group (glycine, alanine, valine, leucine).
- **Acidic** amino acids have an extra carboxyl group, so more $\mathrm{-COOH}$ than $\mathrm{-NH_2}$ (aspartic acid, glutamic acid).
- **Basic** amino acids have an extra amino group or basic group (lysine, arginine, histidine).

**Classification by supply in the diet.** **Essential amino acids** cannot be made by the body and must be taken in food, for example valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine and tryptophan. **Non-essential amino acids** can be synthesised by the body, for example glycine, alanine, aspartic acid and glutamic acid.

**Zwitterion.** In an amino acid the acidic $\mathrm{-COOH}$ transfers a proton to the basic $\mathrm{-NH_2}$ within the same molecule, giving a **dipolar ion** (zwitterion), $\mathrm{R-CH(NH_3^+)-COO^-}$. This is why amino acids are crystalline, have high melting points, dissolve in water and are **amphoteric**. In acid the zwitterion is converted to the cation, in alkali to the anion. At a certain pH, the **isoelectric point**, the net charge is zero and the amino acid does not move in an electric field.
An amino acid exists as a zwitterion in neutral solution.

**Peptide bond.** The carboxyl group of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of another to form an amide link, $\mathrm{-CO-NH-}$, called a **peptide bond**, with loss of water. Two amino acids give a dipeptide, three a tripeptide, and so on. Many (more than about 10) give a polypeptide. A chain of $n$ amino acids contains $n-1$ peptide bonds, and the mass of the peptide is the sum of the masses of the amino acids minus 18 for each water molecule lost.

What to learn from this figure: A peptide bond is an amide link made when the COOH of one amino acid loses OH and the NH2 of the next loses H. Count the bonds as n - 1 and the lost water molecules as n - 1.

blocks.problem: Molar masses: glycine $75\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$ and alanine $89\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$. (a) What is the molar mass of the tripeptide Gly-Ala-Gly? (b) How many peptide bonds does it contain? (c) How many different tripeptides can be formed from three different amino acids if each is used once?
blocks.solution:
(a) The three amino acids have a total mass of $75 + 89 + 75 = 239\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$. Forming the tripeptide needs two condensations, each removing one $\mathrm{H_2O}$ ($18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$), so the molar mass is $239 - 2 \times 18 = 239 - 36 = 203\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$.

(b) The number of peptide bonds is $n - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2$.

(c) The order matters because each peptide has an N-terminal and a C-terminal end. The three different amino acids can be arranged in $3! = 6$ ways, so six tripeptides.

blocks.text: Counting rules: $n$ amino acids give $n-1$ peptide bonds and $n-1$ molecules of water lost. A dipeptide of two *different* amino acids can exist in two forms (Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly) because the sequence matters.
Structure and types of proteins

Proteins are the biomolecules that carry out most of the work of the cell. They are classified in two ways.

**Types by shape.**

- **Fibrous proteins** have long thread-like chains held together side by side by hydrogen and disulfide bonds. They are **insoluble in water** and are structural: keratin (hair, wool, nails) and myosin (muscle).
- **Globular proteins** are folded into a compact, roughly spherical shape, are **soluble in water**, and include most enzymes and many hormones: insulin and albumin.

**Levels of structure.**

1. **Primary structure:** the **sequence** of amino acids in the chain, held by peptide bonds. A change of even one amino acid alters the protein.
2. **Secondary structure:** local folding stabilised by **hydrogen bonds** between the $\mathrm{C=O}$ of one peptide unit and the $\mathrm{N-H}$ of another. Two types: the **$\alpha$-helix** (right-handed coil) and the **$\beta$-pleated sheet** (side-by-side extended chains).
3. **Tertiary structure:** the overall **three-dimensional folding** of one polypeptide chain, stabilised by hydrogen bonds, disulfide bridges, ionic (salt) bridges, van der Waals forces and hydrophobic interactions. This gives the fibrous or globular shape.
4. **Quaternary structure:** the arrangement of **two or more polypeptide subunits** into one functional unit, as in haemoglobin, which has four subunits.

What to learn from this figure: Each level adds a new kind of folding on top of the last: sequence (primary), local H-bonded shapes (secondary), whole-chain 3-D shape (tertiary) and several chains together (quaternary). Only the primary structure is held by covalent peptide bonds.

blocks.text: Denaturation of proteins

The loss of the native three-dimensional structure of a protein (secondary, tertiary and quaternary levels) under the action of heat, a change of pH, or chemicals such as urea, without breaking the peptide bonds, so the **primary structure is unchanged** but the **biological activity is lost**.

The hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that hold the folded protein are disrupted, and the chain unwinds. Examples are the **coagulation of egg white** on boiling and the **curdling of milk**, which is caused by acid produced by bacteria. The protein is often less soluble after denaturation. Denatured enzymes can no longer catalyse reactions, which is why high fever and extreme pH are harmful and why cooking and pasteurising kill microbes.
Denaturation breaks hydrogen and ionic bonds (weak forces), **not** peptide bonds. The primary structure remains. Hydrolysis, by contrast, breaks the peptide bonds.
Enzymes and mechanism of enzyme action

**Enzymes** are biological catalysts that speed up the biochemical reactions of living cells. Almost all are **globular proteins**, and their names usually end with "-ase": invertase hydrolyses sucrose to glucose and fructose, maltase converts maltose to glucose, lactase splits lactose, amylase acts on starch, urease hydrolyses urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide, lipase acts on fats, and zymase converts glucose to ethanol (fermentation). Pepsin (which hydrolyses proteins in the stomach) is an exception to the "-ase" pattern.

**Characteristics of enzymes.**

- **Highly specific:** each acts on one substrate or a group of closely related ones.
- **Very efficient:** a small amount converts a large amount of substrate.
- **Work under mild conditions:** body temperature (about 310 K) and a particular optimum pH, and are destroyed (denatured) by heat or extreme pH.
- Many need a non-protein partner, a **cofactor** or **coenzyme**, and several vitamins act as coenzymes.

**Mechanism of enzyme action (elementary idea).** The enzyme has a specific pocket called the **active site**. The substrate fits into this site (like a key into a lock), forming an **enzyme-substrate complex**. The complex then changes into an enzyme-product complex, which releases the product and the free enzyme, which can be used again. The enzyme provides a pathway with a **lower activation energy**.
E is the enzyme, S the substrate, ES the enzyme-substrate complex and P the product. The enzyme is regenerated.

Enzymes are specific, efficient, work at body temperature and optimum pH, and are inhibited or denatured by heat and extreme pH. The lock-and-key idea explains their specificity: the substrate must complement the shape of the active site.
Vitamins: types, sources and deficiency diseases

An organic compound required in small amounts in the diet for normal growth and health, which the body generally cannot make in sufficient quantity. A lack of a vitamin causes a specific **deficiency disease**.

**Types.** Vitamins are divided by solubility. **Fat-soluble vitamins** (A, D, E and K) are stored in the liver and adipose (fat) tissue. **Water-soluble vitamins** (the B group and C) are excreted in the urine, so they need to be supplied regularly in the diet (vitamin B12 is an exception, since it is stored in the liver).

Nucleic acids: types, composition, structure and biological importance

Nucleic acids are long polymers found in the nucleus of every cell, and are of two **types**: **deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA)** and **ribonucleic acid (RNA)**.

**Composition.** A nucleic acid is a polymer of **nucleotides**, and each nucleotide has three parts: a **phosphate group**, a **pentose sugar** and a **nitrogenous base**. The sugar linked to a base (without the phosphate) is a **nucleoside**.

- The sugar in DNA is **2-deoxy-D-ribose**; in RNA it is **D-ribose**.
- The **purine** bases are **adenine (A)** and **guanine (G)**; the **pyrimidine** bases are **cytosine (C)**, **thymine (T)** and **uracil (U)**.
- DNA contains A, G, C and T. RNA contains A, G, C and **U (uracil instead of thymine)**.

**Structure.** Nucleotides are joined into a chain by **phosphodiester linkages** between the 3' carbon of one sugar and the 5' carbon of the next. **DNA** has the **double helix** structure proposed by Watson and Crick (1953): two polynucleotide strands wind round the same axis in opposite directions, held together by hydrogen bonds between bases. **Adenine pairs only with thymine** by **two** hydrogen bonds, and **guanine pairs only with cytosine** by **three** hydrogen bonds. Therefore in any DNA, A = T and G = C (Chargaff's rule). **RNA** is a single strand and is of three types: **messenger RNA (m-RNA)**, **ribosomal RNA (r-RNA)** and **transfer RNA (t-RNA)**.

**Biological importance.** DNA carries the **genetic information** and passes it from cell to cell and from parent to offspring by **replication**. The information in DNA is read as a sequence of three-base units (codons) and is converted by RNA into the sequence of amino acids of proteins. DNA is therefore the chemical basis of heredity, and RNA is essential for protein synthesis. Studying DNA profiles (DNA fingerprinting) is used in forensic work and in finding paternity.

What to learn from this figure: Pairing is exact: A with T (2 bonds) and G with C (3 bonds). That is why the amount of A equals T and G equals C in any DNA sample, and the two strands are complementary.

blocks.problem: A sample of DNA contains $20\%$ adenine. (a) Find the percentage of thymine, guanine and cytosine. (b) A segment of the DNA has 30 A-T base pairs and 40 G-C base pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together in that segment?
blocks.solution:
(a) By base pairing, adenine pairs with thymine, so thymine is also 20 per cent. Together A + T = 40 per cent, leaving 60 per cent for G + C. Since G pairs with C, they are equal, so G = C = 30 per cent each.

(b) Each A-T pair has 2 hydrogen bonds and each G-C pair has 3. Total hydrogen bonds = $30 \times 2 + 40 \times 3 = 60 + 120 = 180$.

blocks.text: Hormones: classification, biological importance and deficiency diseases
A chemical messenger produced by a ductless (endocrine) gland, secreted directly into the blood and carried to a target organ, where it regulates a particular activity in very small amounts.

**Classification by chemical nature.**

- **Steroid hormones:** testosterone (male sex hormone), estradiol and progesterone (female sex hormones), and the adrenal cortex hormones such as cortisol (glucocorticoids) and aldosterone (mineralocorticoids).
- **Polypeptide (protein) hormones:** insulin and glucagon from the pancreas, oxytocin and vasopressin, and the pituitary hormones, including growth hormone.
- **Amino-acid derivatives:** thyroxine (from the thyroid, contains iodine) and adrenaline (epinephrine, from the adrenal medulla).

diagrams.description: Left: the open-chain Fischer projection of D-glucose with CHO at C-1, then C-2 OH on the right, C-3 OH on the left, C-4 OH on the right, C-5 OH on the right and CH2OH at C-6. A dashed red arrow shows the C-5 hydroxyl attacking C-1. Right: two Haworth drawings of the six-membered pyranose ring (ring oxygen between C-1 and C-5), with OH on C-2 and C-4 pointing down, OH on C-3 pointing up and CH2OH on C-5 pointing up. In alpha-D-glucopyranose the C-1 OH points down (specific rotation +111 degrees); in beta-D-glucopyranose it points up (+19.2 degrees). A box notes that the forms are anomers, that groups on the right of the Fischer chain point down in the ring, and that in water both change to an equilibrium mixture at +52.5 degrees (mutarotation).

diagrams.alt: Glycine and alanine condensing with loss of water to give the dipeptide Gly-Ala, with the peptide bond -CO-NH- highlighted
diagrams.caption: Peptide bond formation between glycine and alanine
diagrams.description: Top: glycine, H2N-CH2-COOH, with its OH circled in red, plus alanine, H2N-CH(CH3)-COOH, with one H of its NH2 circled in red. A downward arrow labelled minus H2O (condensation) leads to the dipeptide H2N-CH2-CO-NH-CH(CH3)-COOH plus H2O. The new -CO-NH- link is boxed and labelled peptide bond; the free NH2 end is labelled N-terminus and the free COOH end C-terminus. A note says n amino acids in a chain contain n minus 1 peptide bonds and release n minus 1 water molecules.

diagrams.alt: Four panels showing primary (a chain of amino acid beads), secondary (alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet), tertiary (one folded chain with bonds) and quaternary (four subunits) protein structure
diagrams.caption: Four levels of protein structure
diagrams.description: Panel 1, primary: six circles labelled Gly, Ala, Ser, Val, Lys, Glu joined by lines (peptide bonds) from the N end to the C end; the sequence is only an example. Panel 2, secondary: a right-handed alpha-helix coil and a beta-pleated sheet of three side-by-side zigzag strands, both with red dashed hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups. Panel 3, tertiary: one polypeptide chain folded into a compact shape with a disulfide bridge (S-S, amber), a hydrogen bond (blue dashed) and an ionic bridge (red dashed), plus van der Waals and hydrophobic forces. Panel 4, quaternary: four subunits (two alpha, two beta, as in haemoglobin) held together by non-covalent forces. All drawings are schematic.

diagrams.alt: Ladder drawing of DNA: two sugar-phosphate backbones joined by four base pairs, A-T and T-A with two hydrogen bonds each and G-C and C-G with three hydrogen bonds each
diagrams.caption: DNA base pairing: A with T (two hydrogen bonds), G with C (three)
diagrams.description: Two vertical sugar-phosphate backbones (S for deoxyribose sugar, P for phosphate), the left running 5 prime to 3 prime from top to bottom and the right running 3 prime to 5 prime, so the strands are opposite in direction. Four horizontal rungs join bases: A-T and T-A each with two dashed hydrogen bonds (blue), then G-C and C-G each with three dashed hydrogen bonds (green). A note says A pairs only with T and G only with C, so A = T and G = C in amount (Chargaff's rule).

questions.stem: Hydrolysis of sucrose with dilute acid gives:
questions.explanation: Sucrose is a disaccharide of alpha-D-glucose and beta-D-fructose joined by an alpha-1,beta-2 glycosidic linkage. Acid or the enzyme invertase breaks that linkage and gives one mole of each monosaccharide, a mixture known as invert sugar because its optical rotation is inverted.

optionRationale.1: Only glucose is obtained from starch, maltose or cellulose, not sucrose.
optionRationale.3: Glucose and galactose are the units of lactose.
optionRationale.4: Fructose is only one half of sucrose.

questions.objective: Recall hydrolysis products of sucrose

questions.stem: Deficiency of which vitamin causes scurvy?
questions.explanation: Scurvy, which shows as bleeding gums and poor wound healing, is caused by lack of vitamin C (ascorbic acid), found in citrus fruits and amla. Vitamin D deficiency gives rickets, vitamin K deficiency delays clotting, and vitamin B1 deficiency causes beriberi.

optionRationale.2: Vitamin K deficiency increases blood clotting time.

questions.objective: Link vitamin C with scurvy

questions.stem: Which nitrogenous base is present in RNA but is absent from DNA?
questions.explanation: DNA contains adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine. In RNA thymine is replaced by uracil, so uracil is present in RNA only. This is one of the main chemical differences between the two nucleic acids, along with the sugar and the number of strands.

optionRationale.2: Thymine is found in DNA, not in RNA.
optionRationale.3: Guanine is a purine present in both DNA and RNA.
optionRationale.4: Adenine is present in both DNA and RNA.

questions.objective: Distinguish the bases of DNA and RNA

questions.stem: The number of peptide bonds in a tetrapeptide is:
questions.explanation: A chain of n amino acids is joined by n - 1 peptide bonds, since each bond joins two neighbouring amino acids. For four amino acids, n - 1 = 3 peptide bonds, and three molecules of water are lost.

optionRationale.1: 2 peptide bonds would join only three amino acids.
optionRationale.2: 4 would be the number of amino acids, not of peptide bonds.
optionRationale.4: 5 is not related to a four-residue peptide.

questions.objective: Count peptide bonds in a peptide

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar.
**Reason (R):** In sucrose the reducing groups of glucose and fructose are involved in the glycosidic linkage.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: In sucrose, C-1 of glucose is bonded to C-2 of fructose, so the anomeric carbons of both units are used in the glycosidic bond. No free hemiacetal group is left to open and give an aldehyde, so sucrose does not reduce Tollens' or Fehling's reagent. The reason correctly explains the assertion.

optionRationale.2: R is not just true but is the direct cause of the non-reducing property.
optionRationale.3: R is also true, so A is true and R is true.
optionRationale.4: A is true: sucrose does not reduce Tollens' reagent.

questions.objective: Explain why sucrose is non-reducing

questions.stem: Enzymes are highly specific in their action because:
options: they are all made of nucleic acids
they are consumed in the reaction
the shape of the active site is complementary to that of the substrate
they work only at very high temperatures
questions.explanation: The active site of an enzyme has a particular shape and arrangement of groups, so only a substrate that fits it can form the enzyme-substrate complex (lock and key idea). The enzyme is regenerated at the end, and works at body temperature.

optionRationale.2: Enzymes are catalysts and are regenerated unchanged.
optionRationale.4: Most enzymes are denatured at high temperatures and work at body temperature.

questions.objective: Explain enzyme specificity using the active site

questions.stem: Maltose is composed of two glucose units linked by:
questions.explanation: Maltose is made of two alpha-D-glucose units connected through C-1 of one and C-4 of the other, an alpha-1,4 linkage. The alpha-1,beta-2 link is in sucrose, beta-1,4 is in lactose and cellulose, and alpha-1,6 appears at branch points in amylopectin and glycogen.

optionRationale.1: Alpha-1,beta-2 is the linkage in sucrose (glucose and fructose).
optionRationale.3: Beta-1,4 is found in lactose and cellulose.
optionRationale.4: Alpha-1,6 appears only at the branch points of amylopectin and glycogen.

questions.objective: Recall the linkage in maltose

questions.stem: Match the vitamin (List-I) with the deficiency disease or symptom (List-II).
questions.explanation: Thiamine (B1) deficiency causes beriberi, vitamin D deficiency causes rickets, vitamin K is needed for blood clotting so its lack increases clotting time, and vitamin B12 deficiency causes pernicious anaemia. Hence A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV.

optionRationale.3: A, B and C are wrongly matched.

questions.objective: Match vitamins with deficiency diseases

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about polysaccharides:
A. Amylose is an unbranched polymer of alpha-D-glucose with alpha-1,4 linkages.
B. Cellulose is a polymer of beta-D-glucose with beta-1,4 linkages.
C. Glycogen is a highly branched polymer of glucose stored in the liver and muscles.
D. Amylopectin is an unbranched polymer that is soluble in water.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: A, B and C are correct facts. D is false: amylopectin is a branched polymer, with alpha-1,6 linkages at branch points, and it is insoluble in water, whereas amylose is the water-soluble linear fraction.

optionRationale.2: D is false, so B, C and D cannot all be true.
optionRationale.3: A is true but D is false.
optionRationale.4: D is false, so not all four are true.

questions.objective: Compare starch, cellulose and glycogen

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Denaturation of a protein destroys its biological activity.
**Reason (R):** Denaturation breaks the peptide bonds and changes the primary structure of the protein.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The assertion is true: when the secondary and tertiary structures are lost, the shape of the active region is lost, so the protein stops working. The reason is false because denaturation disrupts only weak interactions such as hydrogen bonds and ionic bonds. The peptide bonds and thus the primary structure remain intact.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot be the explanation.

questions.objective: Describe what is and is not changed in denaturation

questions.stem: In a DNA double helix, the number of hydrogen bonds between guanine and cytosine is:
questions.explanation: The base pairs in DNA are specific: guanine pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds, and adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds. This is why a G-C rich region is more stable than an A-T rich one.

optionRationale.1: Two is the number of hydrogen bonds between adenine and thymine.
optionRationale.3: One hydrogen bond is not found in either base pair.
optionRationale.4: Four does not match either of the base pairs.

questions.objective: Recall base pairing in DNA

questions.stem: The isoelectric point of an amino acid is the pH at which:
options: the amino acid is completely in the cationic form
the amino acid is completely in the anionic form
the amino acid exists as a zwitterion with zero net charge and does not migrate in an electric field
questions.explanation: At the isoelectric point the positive charge of the ammonium group balances the negative charge of the carboxylate group. The molecule has no net charge and does not move towards either electrode. In more acidic solution it is a cation and in more basic solution an anion.

optionRationale.1: The cation predominates only at low pH.
optionRationale.2: The anion predominates only at high pH.
optionRationale.3: Denaturation applies to proteins and is unrelated to the isoelectric point of a small amino acid.

questions.objective: Define the isoelectric point

questions.stem: Which level of protein structure is retained when a protein is denatured?
questions.explanation: Denaturation disrupts the weak hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions that maintain the folded shape. The peptide bonds are not broken, so the sequence of amino acids, the primary structure, stays unchanged.

optionRationale.2: Secondary structure depends on hydrogen bonds, which are broken.
optionRationale.3: Tertiary structure is lost when the chain unfolds.
optionRationale.4: Quaternary structure, the association of subunits, is also lost.

questions.objective: Identify the structural levels lost in denaturation

questions.stem: Deficiency of insulin causes diabetes mellitus. Insulin is a:
options: steroid hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex
iodine-containing hormone secreted by the thyroid
polypeptide hormone secreted by the pancreas
questions.explanation: Insulin is a protein (polypeptide) hormone made by the pancreas that lowers blood glucose. A lack of it leaves glucose in the blood and causes diabetes mellitus. Steroid hormones come from the adrenal cortex and gonads, and thyroxine is the iodine-containing hormone.

optionRationale.1: Adrenal cortex hormones are steroids, not insulin.
optionRationale.2: Thyroxine is the iodine-containing hormone of the thyroid.
optionRationale.4: Insulin is a polypeptide, not a carbohydrate.

questions.objective: Classify insulin and recall its deficiency disease

questions.stem: Using molar masses of glycine ($75\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$) and alanine ($89\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$), the molar mass of the tripeptide Gly-Ala-Gly is:
questions.explanation: The three amino acids have a combined mass of 75 + 89 + 75 = 239 g/mol. Two peptide bonds form, so two molecules of water (2 x 18 = 36) are lost, and the molar mass is 239 - 36 = 203 g/mol.

optionRationale.1: 239 is the sum of the amino acid masses without subtracting the water.
optionRationale.4: 185 subtracts three water molecules, but there are only two peptide bonds.

questions.objective: Compute the mass of a tripeptide

questions.stem: Sucrose ($[\alpha] = +66.5^\circ$) is hydrolysed; the specific rotations of glucose and fructose are $+52.5^\circ$ and $-92.4^\circ$. The rotation of the equimolar mixture is about:
questions.explanation: The hydrolysis gives equimolar glucose and fructose, so the average rotation is (52.5 - 92.4)/2 = -39.9/2 = -19.95 degrees. The sign changes from + to -, so the mixture is called invert sugar.

optionRationale.2: The sign is wrong: fructose has the larger magnitude of rotation, so the mixture is laevorotatory.
optionRationale.3: -39.9 is the sum and has not been divided by two.
optionRationale.4: -9.98 divides by four instead of by two.

questions.objective: Calculate the rotation of invert sugar

questions.stem: The number of optical isomers of an open-chain aldohexose is:
questions.explanation: An open-chain aldohexose has four stereogenic carbons (C-2, C-3, C-4 and C-5), so it has 2^4 = 16 stereoisomers, 8 of the D-series and 8 of the L-series. A ketohexose such as fructose has only three stereocentres and so has 8.

optionRationale.1: 8 is the number of D-isomers only, or the isomers for three stereocentres as in a ketohexose.
optionRationale.2: 4 is the number of stereocentres, not of isomers.
optionRationale.4: 32 would correspond to five stereocentres, as in the cyclic pyranose forms.

questions.objective: Count optical isomers of a monosaccharide

questions.stem: Match the carbohydrate (List-I) with its composition and linkage (List-II).

right: IV. beta-D-glucose units in a long chain, beta-1,4

questions.explanation: Sucrose is alpha-D-glucose plus beta-D-fructose with an alpha-1,beta-2 link; maltose is two alpha-D-glucose units with alpha-1,4; lactose is beta-D-galactose plus beta-D-glucose with beta-1,4; and cellulose is a chain of beta-D-glucose units with beta-1,4. So A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

optionRationale.3: A and D are swapped, and C is wrongly placed.

questions.objective: Match carbohydrates with their units and linkages

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about nucleic acids:
A. DNA contains 2-deoxy-D-ribose, whereas RNA contains D-ribose.
B. Thymine is present in both DNA and RNA.
C. Adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds and guanine pairs with cytosine through three.
D. Nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester linkages.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: A is true: the sugar of DNA lacks one oxygen at C-2. C is true. D is true because the phosphate links the 3' carbon of one sugar to the 5' carbon of the next. B is false, since RNA has uracil in place of thymine. Therefore A, C and D only.

optionRationale.1: B is false, so A, B and C cannot all be correct.
optionRationale.3: B is false and A and C are true, so this selection is wrong.
optionRationale.4: B is false, so not all four are correct.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on the composition and structure of nucleic acids

questions.stem: A DNA segment has 50 base pairs, of which $40\%$ are G-C pairs. The total number of hydrogen bonds between the two strands is:
questions.explanation: G-C pairs = 40% of 50 = 20, and A-T pairs = 50 - 20 = 30. Each G-C pair has three hydrogen bonds and each A-T pair has two, so the total is 20 x 3 + 30 x 2 = 60 + 60 = 120.

optionRationale.1: 100 would result if every pair were counted as having two hydrogen bonds.
optionRationale.2: 110 does not correspond to the correct counts of either type of pair.
optionRationale.3: 130 results from reversing the bonds (A-T as three and G-C as two) in the count: 20 x 2 + 30 x 3 = 130.

questions.objective: Count hydrogen bonds from base-pair composition
